l: Zedekiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 52
s: Zedekiah began to reign at twenty-one, reigned eleven years in Jerusalem, did evil in the LORD's sight as Jehoiakim had, and rebelled against the king of Babylon. He fled the besieged city by night but was overtaken in the plains of Jericho, taken to Riblah, and judged; his sons were killed before his eyes, his eyes were put out, and he was bound in fetters and imprisoned in Babylon until his death.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 52
s: The LORD's anger is given as the cause of what happened in Jerusalem and Judah, until he had cast the people out from his presence. His house is burned and its vessels carried away to Babylon.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 52
s: Jerusalem was besieged from Zedekiah's ninth year to his eleventh, with severe famine in the city, until a breach was made. Nebuzaradan then burned the LORD's house, the king's house and every great house, and the Chaldeans broke down its walls all around.

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 52
s: Judah's king Zedekiah and its princes were killed or captured, and the chapter concludes that Judah was carried away captive out of its land. Its king Jehoiachin is later released from prison in Babylon.

l: Nebuchadnezzar, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 52
s: Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came with all his army in Zedekiah's ninth year, encamped against Jerusalem and built forts around it. His nineteenth year is when Nebuzaradan entered Jerusalem, and the deportations are dated by his seventh, eighteenth and twenty-third years.

l: Babylon, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 52
s: The king of Babylon besieged Jerusalem, judged Zedekiah at Riblah, killed his sons and the princes of Judah, and imprisoned Zedekiah in Babylon. The bronze of the LORD's house was carried to Babylon, and later its king Evilmerodach released Jehoiachin.

l: Chaldeans, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 52
s: The Chaldeans surrounded the city, pursued King Zedekiah and overtook him in the plains of Jericho, scattering his army. Those with the captain of the guard broke down Jerusalem's walls and broke up the temple's bronze pillars, bases and sea, carrying the bronze to Babylon.

l: Nebuzaradan, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 52
s: Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, came into Jerusalem in the fifth month of Nebuchadnezzar's nineteenth year and burned the LORD's house, the king's house and the great houses. He carried away the poorest and the rest of the people, left some of the poorest as vineyard keepers and farmers, took the temple's gold and silver, and brought Seraiah, Zephaniah and others to Riblah to be put to death. He also carried away 745 Jews in the twenty-third year.

l: siege of Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 52
s: The siege began on the tenth day of the tenth month of Zedekiah's ninth year and lasted to his eleventh year. On the ninth day of the fourth month famine was severe and there was no bread, a breach was made, and the men of war fled by night by the gate between the two walls.

l: the LORD’s house, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 52
s: The LORD's house was burned by Nebuzaradan, and its bronze pillars, bases and bronze sea were broken in pieces by the Chaldeans. The text describes the pillars' dimensions and the capitals with network and pomegranates.

l: temple bronze vessels, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 52
s: The Chaldeans took the two pillars, the sea, the twelve bronze bulls, and the pots, shovels, snuffers, basins and spoons used in ministering, carrying all the bronze to Babylon. The captain of the guard took the gold and silver cups, fire pans, bowls and lamp stands as well; the bronze was beyond weighing.

l: deportations of Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 52
s: Three deportations are counted: 3,023 Jews in Nebuchadnezzar's seventh year, 832 persons from Jerusalem in his eighteenth, and 745 in his twenty-third under Nebuzaradan, for a total of four thousand six hundred. The chapter concludes that Judah was carried away captive out of its land.

l: Jehoiachin, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 52
s: In the thirty-seventh year of his captivity, Jehoiachin king of Judah was released from prison by Evilmerodach, who spoke kindly to him and set his throne above those of the other kings with him in Babylon. He changed his prison garments, ate bread before the king continually, and received a daily allowance until his death.

l: Evilmerodach, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 52
s: Evilmerodach, king of Babylon, in the first year of his reign on the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month, lifted up Jehoiachin's head and released him from prison. He spoke kindly to him, raised his throne above the other kings', and gave him a continual daily allowance for life.

l: The Book of Micah, The Book of Micah, Chapter 1
s: The LORD's word comes to Micah of Morasheth in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, concerning Samaria and Jerusalem. The LORD is called as witness against the peoples and comes down from his holy temple, treading the high places while mountains melt and valleys split. He declares that the disobedience of Jacob and the sins of Israel are embodied in Samaria and Jerusalem, and that Samaria will become a rubble heap with its idols and temple gifts destroyed. Micah laments, wailing and going stripped and naked, because the incurable wound has reached Judah and the gate of Jerusalem. He then names towns such as Gath, Beth Ophrah, Lachish, Moresheth Gath, and Mareshah that will suffer shame, evil, and captivity, and calls on the people to shave their heads for the children taken away.

l: the LORD, The Book of Micah, Chapter 1
s: The LORD's word comes to Micah, and he is summoned as witness against the peoples from his holy temple. He comes down to tread the high places, causing mountains to melt and valleys to split. He declares he will make Samaria a rubble heap, destroy its idols, and bring evil to the gate of Jerusalem.

l: Micah of Morasheth, The Book of Micah, Chapter 1
s: Micah receives the LORD's word in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, concerning Samaria and Jerusalem. He laments and wails, going stripped and naked and howling like jackals, because the wound has reached Judah. He calls on the people to shave their heads in mourning.

l: Judah, The Book of Micah, Chapter 1
s: Judah's kings Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah mark the time of the vision. Its high places are identified with Jerusalem. Samaria's incurable wounds are said to have reached Judah, coming to the gate of the LORD's people.

l: Samaria, The Book of Micah, Chapter 1
s: Samaria is named as the disobedience of Jacob and is a focus of the vision. The LORD will make it a rubble heap like a vineyard planting place, pour its stones into the valley, and uncover its foundations. All its idols will be beaten to pieces and its temple gifts burned.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Micah, Chapter 1
s: Jerusalem is a subject of the vision alongside Samaria and is identified as the high places of Judah. The incurable wound reaches the gate of the people at Jerusalem, and evil from the LORD comes down to its gate.

l: Jacob, The Book of Micah, Chapter 1
s: Jacob's disobedience and the sins of the house of Israel are given as the reason for the coming judgment. The text identifies that disobedience with Samaria.

l: Judgment on Samaria and Judah, The Book of Micah, Chapter 1
s: The LORD comes down in judgment, with mountains melting and valleys splitting, because of the disobedience of Jacob and the sins of Israel. Samaria is to be reduced to rubble with its idols destroyed, and the incurable wound reaches Judah and Jerusalem's gate. Towns such as Lachish, Maroth, and Achzib are affected, and the children of the people go into captivity.

l: The Book of Micah, The Book of Micah, Chapter 2
s: Chapter 2 opens with a woe against those who plot evil at night and carry it out by day, coveting and seizing fields and houses and oppressing people and their heritage. The LORD announces a planned disaster against them, from which they cannot remove their necks, and says they will be mocked with a lament over their divided land and will have no one to assign land by lot in the LORD's assembly. The people tell the prophets not to prophesy, and the text answers by charging that the LORD's people have risen up as an enemy, stripping travelers, driving women from their houses, and taking blessing from children. They are told to depart because their uncleanness destroys, and a lying prophet of wine and strong drink would suit them. The chapter ends with the LORD promising to assemble Jacob and gather the remnant of Israel like sheep, with their king and the LORD at their head breaking through the gate.

l: the LORD, The Book of Micah, Chapter 2
s: The LORD pronounces a woe on oppressors and announces he is planning a disaster against them. He charges his people with acting as an enemy and orders them to depart because their uncleanness destroys. He then promises to assemble Jacob and gather Israel's remnant like sheep, going at the head of them as they break out through the gate.

l: Jacob, The Book of Micah, Chapter 2
s: The house of Jacob is addressed with the questions of whether the LORD's Spirit is angry and whether these are his doings. It is also the one the LORD promises to assemble in full.

l: Israel, The Book of Micah, Chapter 2
s: The LORD promises to gather the remnant of Israel and put them together like the sheep of Bozrah, a flock in the middle of its pasture that swarms with people. Their king passes on before them, with the LORD at their head.

l: those who devise iniquity (oppressors), The Book of Micah, Chapter 2
s: They plan evil on their beds and carry it out at morning light because they have the power to do so. They covet and seize fields and houses and oppress a man along with his house and heritage. The LORD declares a disaster against them, and they will be mocked with a lament over their ruin.

l: my people (the LORD's people), The Book of Micah, Chapter 2
s: The LORD's people are accused of rising up as an enemy, stripping the robe from passersby returning from battle and driving women from their pleasant houses. They take his blessing from the women's young children forever. They are told to arise and depart, since this is not their resting place, and they would favor a prophet who speaks falsely of wine and strong drink.

l: disaster (planned by the LORD), The Book of Micah, Chapter 2
s: The LORD says he is planning a disaster against the oppressors, from which they will not remove their necks. It makes them unable to walk haughtily, since it is an evil time. In that day they will lament that they are utterly ruined and that their fields are assigned to traitors.

l: The Book of Micah, The Book of Micah, Chapter 3
s: The speaker addresses the heads of Jacob and rulers of the house of Israel, accusing them of hating good, loving evil, and brutally devouring the LORD's people, and says the LORD will not answer them when they cry out. The LORD then condemns the prophets who lead his people astray, proclaiming peace for those who feed them and war against those who do not, and declares that night and darkness will fall on them and that they will have no answer from God. The speaker says he is full of power by the LORD's Spirit to declare Jacob's disobedience and Israel's sin. He accuses the rulers of abhorring justice and building Zion and Jerusalem with blood, while leaders, priests, and prophets act for bribes, price, and money yet claim the LORD is among them. The chapter ends with the LORD's pronouncement that Zion will be plowed like a field, Jerusalem will become heaps of rubble, and the temple mountain will be like the high places of a forest.

l: the LORD, The Book of Micah, Chapter 3
s: The LORD will not answer the rulers when they cry to him and will hide his face from them because of their evil deeds. He speaks against the prophets who lead his people astray, sending darkness on them and giving no answer. He empowers the speaker by his Spirit and decrees that Zion will be plowed like a field and Jerusalem become rubble.

l: heads and rulers of Jacob/Israel, The Book of Micah, Chapter 3
s: They are addressed as those who should know justice but instead hate good, love evil, abhor justice, and pervert equity. They are accused of savagely devouring the LORD's people and building Zion with blood and Jerusalem with iniquity. When they cry to the LORD, he will not answer them.

l: Jacob, The Book of Micah, Chapter 3
s: Jacob is addressed through its heads, who are called to listen and to know justice. The speaker is empowered to declare Jacob's disobedience.

l: Israel, The Book of Micah, Chapter 3
s: Israel is addressed through the rulers of its house, who are accused of abhorring justice and perverting equity. The speaker is empowered to declare Israel's sin.

l: my people (the LORD's people), The Book of Micah, Chapter 3
s: The LORD's people are described as being brutalized by their rulers, who tear off their skin, break their bones, and chop them up like meat for the pot. They are also led astray by prophets who proclaim peace for those who feed them.

l: prophets, The Book of Micah, Chapter 3
s: The prophets lead the LORD's people astray, proclaiming "Peace!" to those who feed them and preparing war against those who do not. Their punishment is night with no vision, darkness, and the sun going down on them. The seers and diviners will be disappointed and confounded and will cover their lips because God gives no answer. Her prophets are also said to tell fortunes for money while claiming the LORD is among them.

l: Zion, The Book of Micah, Chapter 3
s: Zion is said to be built up with blood by the rulers. Because of their leaders' corruption, it will be plowed like a field.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Micah, Chapter 3
s: Jerusalem is said to be built up with iniquity, and its leaders judge for bribes, its priests teach for a price, and its prophets divine for money. It will become heaps of rubble, and the temple mountain will be like the high places of a forest.

l: Micah of Morasheth, The Book of Micah, Chapter 3
s: The speaker calls the heads and rulers to listen and challenges them to know justice. He declares himself full of power by the LORD's Spirit, and of judgment and might, to declare Jacob's disobedience and Israel's sin.

l: coming destruction of Zion and Jerusalem, The Book of Micah, Chapter 3
s: The LORD declares that because of the leaders' corruption, Zion will be plowed like a field and Jerusalem will become heaps of rubble. The mountain of the temple will become like the high places of a forest. This answers the leaders' false assurance that no disaster will come on them.

l: The Book of Micah, The Book of Micah, Chapter 4
s: Chapter 4 describes a future time when the mountain of the LORD's temple is exalted and many nations stream to it to learn the LORD's ways, as the law goes out of Zion and the LORD's word from Jerusalem. The LORD judges between peoples, weapons become farming tools, and each person sits secure under vine and fig tree, while his people vow to walk in the LORD's name forever. The LORD promises to gather the lame and driven away of Zion into a remnant and a strong nation, and to reign over them on Mount Zion forever. The daughter of Zion is told the former dominion will return, yet she must first endure labor pains, leave the city, and go to Babylon, where the LORD will redeem her from her enemies. Many nations gather against Zion to gloat, not knowing the LORD has gathered them like sheaves to the threshing floor, and Zion is commanded to arise and thresh them with iron horn and bronze hoofs.

l: the LORD, The Book of Micah, Chapter 4
s: The LORD is said to establish his temple mountain, teach many nations his ways, and judge between peoples and strong nations. He promises to gather the lame and driven away, make them a strong nation, and reign over them on Mount Zion forever. He will redeem Zion from her enemies in Babylon, has gathered hostile nations like sheaves to the threshing floor, and will give Zion an iron horn and bronze hoofs, claiming their gain for himself as Lord of the whole earth.

l: Zion, The Book of Micah, Chapter 4
s: Zion is the place from which the law goes out, and the mountain where the LORD will reign forever. Addressed as the daughter of Zion, she is promised the return of her former dominion, told to labor in pain, leave the city, and go to Babylon where she will be rescued. She is then commanded to arise and thresh many peoples who gather to defile her and gloat over her.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Micah, Chapter 4
s: Jerusalem is the source from which the LORD's word goes out. It is called the seat of the kingdom of the daughter of Jerusalem, whose former dominion will come again.

l: mountain of the LORD's temple, The Book of Micah, Chapter 4
s: In the latter days this mountain will be established on the top of the mountains and exalted above the hills. Peoples will stream to it, and many nations will say they will go up to it to be taught the God of Jacob's ways.

l: nations, The Book of Micah, Chapter 4
s: Many nations will go up to the LORD's mountain to be taught his ways and be judged by him, and will no longer lift sword against each other or learn war. Though all nations walk in the name of their gods, other nations also assemble against Zion to defile her and gloat, not understanding the LORD's counsel. He has gathered them like sheaves to the threshing floor, where Zion will beat many peoples in pieces.

l: Babylon, The Book of Micah, Chapter 4
s: Babylon is the place Zion will come to after leaving the city and dwelling in the field. There the LORD will rescue and redeem her from the hand of her enemies.

l: remnant of Jacob, The Book of Micah, Chapter 4
s: The LORD will assemble the lame and gather the driven away, including those he has afflicted. He will make the lame a remnant and those cast far off a strong nation, over whom he will reign on Mount Zion forever.

l: swords and spears turned to farming tools, The Book of Micah, Chapter 4
s: When the LORD judges between many peoples and strong nations, they will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation will not lift sword against nation, nor learn war any more, and everyone will sit unafraid under vine and fig tree.

l: The Book of Micah, The Book of Micah, Chapter 5
s: Chapter 5 describes a besieged Israel whose judge is struck on the cheek, then promises a ruler from Bethlehem Ephrathah whose origins are ancient and who will shepherd in the strength of the LORD and be great to the ends of the earth. He will be peace and deliver the people from Assyria, whose land will be ruled with the sword by seven shepherds and eight leaders of men. The remnant of Jacob is pictured both as dew and showers among many peoples and as a lion among the animals of the forest that tramples and tears with no one to deliver. The LORD declares that he will cut off Israel's horses, chariots, cities and strongholds, and destroy witchcraft, soothsayers, engraved images, pillars and Asherah poles. He will execute vengeance in anger and wrath on the nations that did not listen.

l: Bethlehem Ephrathah, The Book of Micah, Chapter 5
s: Bethlehem Ephrathah is addressed as small among the clans of Judah. Out of it one will come to be ruler in Israel for the LORD.

l: ruler in Israel, The Book of Micah, Chapter 5
s: The ruler in Israel will come out of Bethlehem Ephrathah, and his goings out are from of old, from ancient times. He will stand and shepherd in the strength and majesty of the name of the LORD his God, and will be great to the ends of the earth. He will be peace and deliver the people from the Assyrian.

l: Israel, The Book of Micah, Chapter 5
s: Israel is besieged, and its judge will be struck with a rod on the cheek. The LORD will abandon them until she who is in labor gives birth, after which the rest of the ruler's brothers will return to the children of Israel. The LORD will also cut off its horses, chariots, cities and strongholds.

l: the LORD, The Book of Micah, Chapter 5
s: The LORD gives strength and majesty to the coming ruler and is the source of the dew-like remnant's blessing. He declares that he will cut off horses, chariots, cities and strongholds, destroy witchcraft and idols, and execute vengeance in anger and wrath on the nations that did not listen.

l: Assyria, The Book of Micah, Chapter 5
s: Assyria is described as invading the land and marching through its fortresses. In response seven shepherds and eight leaders of men will be raised against it, and they will rule the land of Assyria with the sword and the land of Nimrod in its gates. The ruler will deliver the people from the Assyrian.

l: remnant of Jacob, The Book of Micah, Chapter 5
s: The remnant of Jacob will be among many peoples like dew from the LORD and like showers on the grass, which do not wait for man. It will also be among the nations like a lion among forest animals or a young lion among flocks of sheep, treading down and tearing in pieces with no one to deliver.

l: nations, The Book of Micah, Chapter 5
s: The nations are those among whom the remnant of Jacob will live, like a lion among them. The LORD will execute vengeance in anger and wrath on the nations that did not listen.

l: idolatry and witchcraft, The Book of Micah, Chapter 5
s: The LORD says he will destroy witchcraft from the people's hand and leave them no soothsayers. He will also cut off engraved images and pillars so that they no longer worship the work of their hands, and will uproot the Asherah poles.

l: The Book of Micah, The Book of Micah, Chapter 6
s: The LORD summons Israel to plead a case before the mountains and hills, which are called to hear his indictment of his people. He asks what he has done to burden them and recalls bringing them out of Egypt and sending Moses, Aaron, and Miriam, as well as his dealings with Balak king of Moab and Balaam son of Beor. A speaker asks how to approach the exalted God, wondering about burnt offerings, calves, thousands of rams, rivers of oil, or even a firstborn, and is told that the LORD has shown what is good: to act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with God. The LORD's voice then calls to the city, charging it with treasures of wickedness, a short ephah, dishonest scales, deceitful weights, and violent, lying rich men. He announces that he has struck and desolated them, that they will eat without being satisfied, sow without reaping, and be made a ruin and a hissing for following the statutes of Omri and the works of Ahab's house.

l: the LORD, The Book of Micah, Chapter 6
s: The LORD calls the mountains and hills to witness his indictment, asks what he has done to burden his people, and recalls redeeming them from Egypt and sending Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. He declares what is good and what he requires, accuses the city of dishonesty and violence, and announces that he has struck and desolated it for its sins.

l: Israel, The Book of Micah, Chapter 6
s: Israel is the people with whom the LORD contends and who are told to remember their redemption from Egypt and the episode of Balak and Balaam. Because they keep the statutes of Omri and the works of Ahab's house, they are threatened with ruin and with bearing reproach.

l: the LORD's case against Israel, The Book of Micah, Chapter 6
s: The LORD summons Israel to plead before the mountains and hills and calls the enduring foundations of the earth to hear his indictment. He bases it on his saving acts, asks what he has done to burden them, and charges them with wickedness, dishonest scales, violence, lies, and following the ways of Omri and Ahab's house.

l: offerings and sacrifices, The Book of Micah, Chapter 6
s: A speaker asks whether burnt offerings, year-old calves, thousands of rams, tens of thousands of rivers of oil, or even a firstborn child could win the LORD's favor. The answer given is not a sacrifice but a statement of what is good, which implies these are not what the LORD requires.

l: what the LORD requires (justice, mercy, humility), The Book of Micah, Chapter 6
s: The text says the LORD has shown humanity what is good and that he requires three things: to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with God. This is given in answer to the question about offerings.

l: the city, The Book of Micah, Chapter 6
s: The LORD's voice calls to the city, and wisdom is said to fear his name. The city is charged with treasures of wickedness, a short ephah, dishonest scales, and deceitful weights, and its inhabitants speak lies and are threatened with becoming a ruin and a hissing.

l: dishonest commerce, The Book of Micah, Chapter 6
s: The LORD asks whether he can tolerate treasures of wickedness, an accursed short ephah, dishonest scales, and a bag of deceitful weights. These practices are named among the sins for which the city is punished.

l: rich men of the city, The Book of Micah, Chapter 6
s: The rich men of the city are described as full of violence. Their inhabitants speak lies and have deceitful tongues, and these are among the grounds for the LORD's judgment.

l: the LORD's punishment, The Book of Micah, Chapter 6
s: The LORD says he has struck the city with a grievous wound and made it desolate because of its sins. He foretells that they will eat without being satisfied, store up without saving, sow without reaping, tread olives without anointing with oil, and crush grapes without drinking wine, and that what they save will go to the sword. He adds that he will make them a ruin and a hissing, and they will bear reproach.

l: The Book of Micah, The Book of Micah, Chapter 7
s: The speaker laments that the godly have vanished from the land and that corruption, bribery, violence, and betrayal reach even into families and close friendships. Despite this, the speaker resolves to look to the LORD, confessing sin and bearing the LORD's indignation until the LORD pleads his case, brings him into the light, and shames the enemy who asked 'Where is the LORD your God?' The text then promises a day of rebuilt walls, extended boundaries, and people coming from Assyria, Egypt, and beyond, though the land will also be desolate because of its inhabitants' deeds. It closes with a prayer that the LORD shepherd his people as in the days of coming out of Egypt, with the nations ashamed and trembling, and praises the LORD as a God who pardons iniquity, delights in loving kindness, and keeps his oath to Jacob and Abraham.

l: the LORD, The Book of Micah, Chapter 7
s: The LORD is the one the speaker waits for as the God of his salvation, who will hear him, be a light in darkness, plead his case, and execute judgment. He is asked to shepherd his people and show marvelous things as in the days of Egypt, and is praised as incomparable: he pardons iniquity, does not retain anger forever, delights in loving kindness, treads iniquities underfoot, casts sins into the sea, and keeps his sworn promise to the fathers.

l: Micah of Morasheth, The Book of Micah, Chapter 7
s: The speaker cries 'Misery is mine!' over a land where the godly are gone and trust is impossible even among family. He resolves to look to the LORD and wait, acknowledges that he has sinned and will bear the LORD's indignation, and expects to rise after falling and to see the LORD's righteousness. He also prays for the LORD to shepherd his people.

l: Israel, The Book of Micah, Chapter 7
s: The LORD's people are called his flock and heritage, dwelling by themselves in a forest, and are asked to be fed in Bashan and Gilead as in days of old. They are promised rebuilt walls, an extended boundary, and a gathering from Assyria, Egypt, and from sea to sea and mountain to mountain. Yet the land will be desolate because of its inhabitants' deeds, and the remnant is shown compassion and promised truth and mercy as sworn to their fathers.

l: wicked men of the land, The Book of Micah, Chapter 7
s: The wicked are described as lying in wait for blood, hunting one another with nets, and doing evil diligently. The ruler and judge ask for bribes, the powerful dictate their evil desires, and even the best among them are like a brier or thorn hedge. Their day of visitation and confusion has come, and the land will be desolate because of the fruit of their doings.

l: enemy (who said 'Where is the LORD your God?'), The Book of Micah, Chapter 7
s: The enemy, referred to as 'her', is told not to rejoice over the speaker's fall, since he will arise. She taunted, 'Where is the LORD your God?', but the speaker expects her to see the LORD's vindication, be covered with shame, and be trodden down like the mire of the streets.

l: restoration and regathering, The Book of Micah, Chapter 7
s: The unit promises a day to build walls and extend boundaries, when people will come from Assyria, the cities of Egypt, the River, and from sea to sea and mountain to mountain. It also expects the LORD to show marvelous things as in the exodus from Egypt, with the nations ashamed, silenced, and coming trembling to the LORD in fear.

l: Israel's sins and God's forgiveness, The Book of Micah, Chapter 7
s: The speaker admits having sinned against the LORD and accepts his indignation until the LORD pleads his case. The unit then praises the LORD as a God who pardons iniquity and passes over the disobedience of the remnant, who does not keep anger forever, and who will have compassion again, tread iniquities underfoot, and cast all sins into the depths of the sea.

l: The Book of Nahum, The Book of Nahum, The Book of Nahum / Chapter 1
s: Chapter 1 of Nahum opens as a revelation about Nineveh, given through Nahum the Elkoshite. It portrays the LORD as a jealous, avenging God who is slow to anger yet great in power, whose presence makes the sea, rivers, mountains, and earth quake and wither. The LORD is described as a stronghold for those who take refuge in him, but he will make a full end of the place of his enemies with an overflowing flood and pursue them into darkness. The LORD addresses one party, promising to break the yoke and bonds laid on them, and pronounces doom on another: no descendants will bear its name, its idols will be cut off, and a grave will be made for it. The chapter ends with a messenger on the mountains announcing peace and telling Judah to keep its feasts and vows, because the wicked one is utterly cut off.

l: LORD of Armies, The Book of Nahum, The Book of Nahum / Chapter 1
s: The LORD is portrayed as a jealous, avenging God, slow to anger and great in power, who will not leave the guilty unpunished and who commands the whirlwind, storm, sea, and rivers. He is a stronghold for those who take refuge in him, will end his enemies with an overflowing flood, and promises to break the yoke from the afflicted and to cut off the descendants and images of the one he condemns.

l: Nineveh, The Book of Nahum, The Book of Nahum / Chapter 1
s: Nineveh is the subject of the revelation that opens the book. The chapter's closing oracles describe a doomed party addressed as "you": it will have no more descendants to bear its name, its engraved and molten images will be cut off from the house of its gods, and the LORD will make its grave because it is vile. The text does not name Nineveh again after verse 1.

l: Judah, The Book of Nahum, The Book of Nahum / Chapter 1
s: Judah is told to keep its feasts and perform its vows, because the wicked one will no more pass through it and is utterly cut off. A messenger bringing good news and publishing peace is seen on the mountains. The promise that the LORD will break the yoke and bonds and afflict "you" no more may also concern Judah, though the text does not name the addressee.

l: adversaries of the LORD, The Book of Nahum, The Book of Nahum / Chapter 1
s: The LORD takes vengeance on his adversaries and maintains wrath against his enemies, pursuing them into darkness and making a full end of their place with an overflowing flood. Those who plot against him are told affliction will not rise a second time, and they are likened to entangled thorns, drunkards, and dry stubble that is consumed utterly. Even at full strength and in great numbers they will be cut down and pass away, and one who devises evil and counsels wickedness against the LORD has gone out of the addressed party.

l: The Book of Nahum, The Book of Nahum, Chapter 2
s: Chapter 2 describes an attacker, called 'he who dashes in pieces', advancing against Nineveh, and the city is told to guard its fortress and strengthen itself. The attacking army is shown with red shields, scarlet-clad warriors, and flashing chariots that rage through the streets. Nineveh's defense collapses: the river gates open, the palace dissolves, and the people flee while the city is plundered of silver and gold and left empty, void, and waste. The text asks where the lions' den has gone, recalling how the lion once tore prey for his cubs and lionesses with no one to make them afraid. The LORD of Armies declares that he is against Nineveh, and says he will burn her chariots, cut the sword through her young lions, cut off her prey, and silence her messengers.

l: LORD of Armies, The Book of Nahum, Chapter 2
s: The LORD of Armies declares, 'Behold, I am against you,' addressing Nineveh. He announces that he will burn her chariots in smoke, have the sword devour her young lions, cut off her prey from the earth, and end the voice of her messengers. Earlier, it is said that the LORD restores the excellency of Jacob as the excellency of Israel.

l: Nineveh, The Book of Nahum, Chapter 2
s: Nineveh is ordered to prepare its defenses but is overwhelmed: the river gates are opened, the palace dissolves, and the city is uncovered and carried away. Though it has been like a pool of water from of old, its people flee without looking back, its treasures of silver and gold are plundered, and it is left empty, void, and waste. The LORD of Armies declares himself against it.

l: he who dashes in pieces (the attacker of Nineveh), The Book of Nahum, Chapter 2
s: He has come up against Nineveh, and his force is described with red shields, scarlet-clad valiant men, and flashing chariots in the day of his preparation. His chariots rage through the streets like torches and lightning, and he summons his picked troops, who rush to the wall and set up the protective shield. His assault leads to the city's collapse and plunder.

l: lion (Nineveh's den), The Book of Nahum, Chapter 2
s: The lion, with his lioness and cubs, is pictured as living in a den where no one made them afraid. He tore prey in pieces for his cubs and lionesses and filled his caves and dens with the kill. The text asks where this den now is, and the LORD of Armies declares that the sword will devour the young lions and that he will cut off their prey from the earth.

l: fall of Nineveh, The Book of Nahum, Chapter 2
s: The fall is portrayed through the attacker's assault, with chariots in the streets, the opening of the river gates, and the dissolving of the palace. The city is decreed uncovered and carried away, its servants moan like doves, its people flee, and its treasure is plundered, leaving it empty, void, and waste. The LORD of Armies' declaration that he is against Nineveh frames the destruction.

l: The Book of Nahum, The Book of Nahum, Chapter 3
s: Chapter 3 pronounces woe on the bloody city, Nineveh, describing its lies, robbery, chariots, slaughter, and heaps of corpses, and blaming its prostitution and witchcraft that sell nations and families. The LORD of Armies declares he is against the city and will expose its nakedness and shame, make it a spectacle, and leave it with no one to mourn or comfort it. Nineveh is compared to No-Amon, which had water, Cush, Egypt, Put, and Libya for defense yet was carried into captivity, its children dashed to pieces and its great men chained. Nineveh's fortresses are said to fall like ripe figs, its troops are women, its gates are open, and fire and sword will devour it despite preparations for siege. The chapter ends by addressing the king of Assyria, whose shepherds slumber and whose people are scattered, with a wound that cannot be healed and that all who hear of it greet by clapping because of his endless cruelty.

l: Nineveh, The Book of Nahum, Chapter 3
s: Nineveh is called the bloody city, full of lies and robbery, and is accused of prostitution and witchcraft that sell nations and families. The LORD of Armies declares he is against it and will expose its shame and make it a spectacle, while onlookers flee and say it is laid waste with no one to mourn. Its fortresses will fall like ripe figs, its troops are women, its gates are open, and fire and sword will devour it despite its siege preparations.

l: LORD of Armies, The Book of Nahum, Chapter 3
s: The LORD of Armies speaks against Nineveh, saying he is against it. He promises to lift its skirts over its face, show the nations its nakedness and the kingdoms its shame, throw abominable filth on it, and make it a spectacle.

l: No-Amon, The Book of Nahum, Chapter 3
s: No-Amon is presented as a comparison for Nineveh: it was situated among rivers, had the sea as its rampart and wall, and had Cush, Egypt, Put, and Libya as strength and helpers. Even so it was carried into captivity, its young children dashed in pieces at the head of the streets, lots cast for its honorable men, and its great men bound in chains.

l: king of Assyria, The Book of Nahum, Chapter 3
s: The king of Assyria is addressed directly: his shepherds slumber, his nobles lie down, and his people are scattered on the mountains with no one to gather them. His wound is said to be beyond healing and fatal, and all who hear of it clap their hands because of his endless cruelty.

l: Nineveh's violence and bloodshed, The Book of Nahum, Chapter 3
s: The chapter opens with images of violence: the whip, rattling wheels, prancing horses, bounding chariots, charging horsemen, flashing swords, glittering spears, and endless heaps of corpses over which people stumble. The city is accused of lies and robbery with no end to its prey, and the king of Assyria's endless cruelty is felt by all.

l: fall of Nineveh, The Book of Nahum, Chapter 3
s: The fall is foretold: the city will be laid waste, its fortresses will fall like ripe figs shaken into the eater's mouth, and its gates stand open to enemies. Fire and sword will devour it, its guards and officials will flee like locusts when the sun appears, and its wound is declared incurable, with its people scattered.

l: Habakkuk, Habakkuk, The Book of Habakkuk / Chapter 1
s: The prophet Habakkuk receives a revelation and cries out to the LORD, asking how long he must call for help against violence, iniquity, and perverted justice while the wicked surround the righteous. The LORD answers that he is raising up the Chaldeans, a bitter, hasty, and feared nation that marches across the earth seizing dwellings that are not theirs, mocking kings and strongholds, and taking prisoners like sand. The Chaldeans are called guilty because their strength is their god. Habakkuk responds by affirming that the LORD is everlasting and has appointed them for judgment, yet he questions why the LORD, whose eyes are too pure to look on evil, tolerates treachery and is silent when the wicked swallow up those more righteous. He closes by describing the oppressor as a fisherman who nets people, sacrifices to his net, and lives luxuriously, and asks whether he will keep emptying his net and killing nations without mercy.

l: Habakkuk, Habakkuk, The Book of Habakkuk / Chapter 1
s: Habakkuk the prophet sees a revelation and cries to the LORD about violence, iniquity, and the failure of justice. After the LORD's answer, he affirms that the LORD is everlasting and has appointed the Chaldeans for judgment, but he questions why the LORD tolerates treachery and stays silent, and asks whether the oppressor will keep killing nations without mercy.

l: LORD, Habakkuk, The Book of Habakkuk / Chapter 1
s: The LORD is accused by Habakkuk of not hearing or saving and of showing him iniquity. He answers that he is working a work in their days that people will not believe, raising up the Chaldeans. Habakkuk calls him everlasting, his Holy One and Rock, with eyes too pure to see evil, who has appointed the Chaldeans to judge and punish.

l: Chaldeans, Habakkuk, The Book of Habakkuk / Chapter 1
s: The LORD says he is raising up the Chaldeans, a bitter and hasty nation that marches across the earth to possess dwellings not theirs. They are feared and dreaded, with swift horses and horsemen who fly like an eagle to devour, gather prisoners like sand, and scoff at kings and strongholds. They are called guilty because their strength is their god, and Habakkuk says they are appointed for judgment and to punish.

l: the wicked, Habakkuk, The Book of Habakkuk / Chapter 1
s: The wicked surround the righteous, so that justice comes out perverted. Habakkuk complains that the LORD keeps silent while the wicked swallows up a man more righteous than he, and he describes the oppressor netting people like fish, rejoicing, sacrificing to his net, and living luxuriously by it.

l: the righteous, Habakkuk, The Book of Habakkuk / Chapter 1
s: The righteous are surrounded by the wicked, and as a result justice is perverted. Habakkuk laments that a man more righteous than the wicked one is swallowed up while the LORD is silent.

l: violence and injustice, Habakkuk, The Book of Habakkuk / Chapter 1
s: Habakkuk cries out about violence, iniquity, perversity, destruction, strife, and contention, which are before him. He says the law is paralyzed and justice never prevails, and the Chaldeans are said to come all of them for violence.

l: Habakkuk, Habakkuk, Chapter 2
s: The speaker takes a watchman's post to await the LORD's answer to his complaint. The LORD tells him to write the vision plainly on tablets and to wait for it, since it will surely come at its appointed time, and that the righteous will live by faith. The LORD then pronounces a series of woes on an arrogant, insatiable man who plunders nations, enriches himself by extortion, builds cities with blood, and shames his own house, warning that the plundered peoples will rise and plunder him. The passage also condemns the one who makes his neighbor drunk to gaze on his nakedness, and the maker who trusts in lifeless idols of wood and stone overlaid with gold and silver. It closes by declaring that the earth will be filled with knowledge of the LORD's glory and that the LORD is in his holy temple, before whom all the earth must be silent.

l: LORD, Habakkuk, Chapter 2
s: The LORD answers the speaker's complaint, instructing him to write the vision and wait for it. He pronounces woes on the oppressor, promises that the earth will be filled with knowledge of his glory as waters cover the sea, and declares that he is in his holy temple, calling all the earth to silence before him. The text also says the peoples' labor for the fire and vanity comes from him, and that the cup of his right hand will come around to the oppressor.

l: Habakkuk, Habakkuk, Chapter 2
s: The speaker stands at his watch on the ramparts, looking out to see what the LORD will say to him and how he should answer concerning his complaint. He receives the LORD's reply and is told to write the vision plainly on tablets.

l: arrogant man (the oppressor), Habakkuk, Chapter 2
s: He is described as puffed up, not upright, treacherous through wine, and as enlarging his desire like Sheol, never satisfied, gathering all nations to himself. He is the target of repeated woes for extortion, evil gain, building a city with blood, and shaming his house, and the text says the peoples will take up a taunting proverb against him and his debtors and the plundered will rise and plunder him. He will also drink the cup of the LORD's right hand, be exposed, and be covered with disgrace.

l: vision, Habakkuk, Chapter 2
s: The vision is to be written plainly on tablets so that one who runs may read it. It is for the appointed time, hurries toward the end, won't prove false, and will surely come without delay, so the speaker must wait for it.

l: nations and peoples, Habakkuk, Chapter 2
s: The nations and peoples have been plundered and gathered up by the oppressor, but the remnant of the peoples will plunder him in return. The text says they labor for the fire and weary themselves for vanity, and that the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the LORD's glory.

l: idols, Habakkuk, Chapter 2
s: The engraved and molten images are called worthless and a teacher of lies, made mute by their makers who trust in them. A woe falls on whoever says to wood 'Awake!' or to mute stone 'Arise!', since an idol overlaid with gold and silver has no breath within it, in contrast to the LORD in his holy temple.

l: bloodshed and violence, Habakkuk, Chapter 2
s: Men's blood and violence done to the land, cities, Lebanon, and the animals are named as the grounds on which the oppressor will be plundered and overwhelmed. The text condemns building a town with blood, and says the stone and beam of the house will cry out in witness.

l: Habakkuk, Habakkuk, Chapter 3
s: Chapter 3 is a prayer of Habakkuk the prophet, set to victorious music. Habakkuk asks the LORD to renew his work and to remember mercy in wrath, then recalls God's awesome coming from Teman and Mount Paran, with plague, shaking earth, trembling nations and mountains, and rivers and sea stirred as God marched in wrath. God went out to save his people and his anointed, crushing the land of wickedness and piercing the heads of its warriors with their own spears. Habakkuk trembles and must wait quietly for the day of trouble when invaders come, yet he resolves to rejoice in the LORD even if fig trees, vines, olives, fields, flocks, and herds all fail. He ends by declaring that God is his strength, making his feet like deer's feet and enabling him to walk in high places.

l: LORD, Habakkuk, Chapter 3
s: The LORD is praised as coming from Teman and Mount Paran, his glory covering the heavens and his praise filling the earth, with plague and pestilence going before and after him. He shakes the earth, makes the nations tremble, rides on horses and chariots of salvation, marches in wrath, and goes out to save his people and his anointed by crushing the land of wickedness. Habakkuk asks him to renew his work and remember mercy in wrath, and declares him his strength and the God of his salvation.

l: Habakkuk, Habakkuk, Chapter 3
s: Habakkuk, called the prophet, offers this prayer, stands in awe of the LORD's deeds, and asks him to renew his work. He trembles in body and lips, feels rottenness in his bones, and must wait quietly for the day of trouble. He nevertheless resolves to rejoice in the LORD and declares that God makes his feet like deer's feet and lets him go in high places.

l: nations, Habakkuk, Chapter 3
s: The nations tremble when the LORD looks at them, and he threshes them in anger as he marches through the land in wrath. The ancient mountains crumble and the age-old hills collapse before him. The tents of Cushan are seen in affliction and the dwellings of Midian tremble.

l: people (God's people), Habakkuk, Chapter 3
s: The LORD goes out for the salvation of his people and his anointed. Habakkuk, speaking for them, says he must wait quietly for the day of trouble, when the people who invade them come up. The invaders' warriors come like a whirlwind to scatter them, but are pierced with their own spears.

l: famine of the land, Habakkuk, Chapter 3
s: Habakkuk describes a possible famine in which the fig tree does not flourish, there is no fruit on the vines, the olive crop fails, the fields yield no food, the flocks are cut off from the fold, and the stalls hold no herd. Even in such lack, he says he will rejoice in the LORD and be joyful in the God of his salvation.

l: Habakkuk's prayer, Habakkuk, Chapter 3
s: The prayer is labeled a prayer of Habakkuk the prophet, set to victorious music, and closes with a note for the music director on stringed instruments. It moves from a plea for renewed work and mercy, through a vision of God's powerful coming and victory, to Habakkuk's fear and finally his joyful trust in the LORD as his strength.

l: The Book of Zephaniah, The Book of Zephaniah, The Book of Zephaniah / Chapter 1
s: The word of the LORD comes to Zephaniah in the days of Josiah, king of Judah. The LORD announces he will sweep away everything from the earth, including man, animal, birds and fish, and will stretch out his hand against Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, cutting off the remnant of Baal and those who worship the sky's army, swear by Malcam, or have turned from him. He declares that the day of the LORD is at hand, with a sacrifice prepared, and that he will punish princes, the king's sons, and the violent and deceitful. He will search Jerusalem with lamps to punish those complacent on their dregs, whose wealth will be plundered. The great day of the LORD is described as a day of wrath, darkness, and alarm, when sinful men will be unable to be saved by silver or gold and the whole land will be devoured by the fire of his jealousy.

l: the LORD, The Book of Zephaniah, The Book of Zephaniah / Chapter 1
s: The LORD speaks through Zephaniah, vowing to sweep away everything from the earth and to stretch out his hand against Judah and Jerusalem. He prepares a sacrifice, will search Jerusalem with lamps, punishes the wicked, and will make a terrible end of all who dwell in the land in the fire of his jealousy.

l: Judah, The Book of Zephaniah, The Book of Zephaniah / Chapter 1
s: Judah is ruled by King Josiah, son of Amon, when the word comes to Zephaniah. The LORD declares he will stretch out his hand against Judah and cut off the remnant of Baal and the idolatrous priests from it.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Zephaniah, The Book of Zephaniah / Chapter 1
s: Jerusalem is the place from which the LORD will cut off the remnant of Baal. He says he will search it with lamps, and cries and wailing are described from its fish gate, second quarter, and hills.

l: inhabitants of Jerusalem, The Book of Zephaniah, The Book of Zephaniah / Chapter 1
s: The LORD says he will stretch out his hand against all the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Those among them who worship the sky's army, swear by Malcam, leap over the threshold, or fill their master's house with violence and deceit are marked for punishment.

l: day of the LORD's judgment, The Book of Zephaniah, The Book of Zephaniah / Chapter 1
s: The day of the LORD is announced as at hand, near, and hurrying greatly, and is called the day of the LORD's sacrifice. It is described as a day of wrath, distress, anguish, trouble, ruin, darkness, gloom, clouds, blackness, trumpet and alarm against fortified cities, in which silver and gold cannot deliver anyone.

l: men settled on their dregs, The Book of Zephaniah, The Book of Zephaniah / Chapter 1
s: These men say in their heart that the LORD will neither do good nor evil. The LORD says he will search Jerusalem with lamps to punish them, and that their wealth will be plundered, their houses desolated, and they will build houses and plant vineyards without enjoying them.

l: sinful men, The Book of Zephaniah, The Book of Zephaniah / Chapter 1
s: Because they have sinned against the LORD, the LORD will bring such distress on men that they walk like blind men. Their blood will be poured out like dust and their flesh like dung, and neither silver nor gold will deliver them.

l: man and animal, The Book of Zephaniah, The Book of Zephaniah / Chapter 1
s: The LORD says he will sweep away man and animal, along with the birds of the sky and the fish of the sea, and the heaps of rubble with the wicked. He also says he will cut off man from the surface of the earth.

l: earth, The Book of Zephaniah, The Book of Zephaniah / Chapter 1
s: The LORD vows to utterly sweep away everything from the surface of the earth. He will cut man off from it, and the whole land will be devoured by the fire of his jealousy.

l: The Book of Zephaniah, The Book of Zephaniah, Chapter 2
s: Chapter 2 opens with a call for the shameless nation to gather and for the humble of the land to seek the LORD, righteousness, and humility before the day of the LORD's anger arrives. The LORD then announces destruction on the Philistine cities of Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, and Ekron, whose coast will become pasture for the remnant of the house of Judah. Moab and the children of Ammon will become like Sodom and Gomorrah for reproaching and magnifying themselves against the LORD's people, whose remnant will plunder and inherit them. The LORD will also strike the Cushites and stretch out his hand against Assyria, making Nineveh a desolation inhabited by animals. Nineveh is portrayed as the carefree city that claimed 'I am, and there is no one besides me,' and will now be mocked by all who pass.

l: the LORD, The Book of Zephaniah, Chapter 2
s: The LORD urges the humble to seek him and warns of his coming anger. He declares destruction on the Philistines, Moab, Ammon, the Cushites, and Assyria, and promises to visit and restore the remnant of Judah. He will be awesome to the nations, famishing the gods of the land so that men worship him from every place.

l: Philistines, The Book of Zephaniah, Chapter 2
s: The Philistines, called the nation of the Cherethites and the inhabitants of the sea coast, are told the LORD's word is against them. Gaza will be forsaken, Ashkelon desolate, Ashdod driven out, and Ekron rooted up, until no inhabitant remains. Their coast will become pastures and folds for shepherds.

l: house of Judah, The Book of Zephaniah, Chapter 2
s: The remnant of the house of Judah will receive the Philistine coast as pasture and will lie down in the houses of Ashkelon in the evening. The LORD, their God, will visit and restore them.

l: Moab, The Book of Zephaniah, Chapter 2
s: Moab is accused of reproaching the LORD's people and magnifying itself against their border. Out of pride it will become like Sodom, a possession of nettles and salt pits and a perpetual desolation, plundered by the remnant of the LORD's people.

l: children of Ammon, The Book of Zephaniah, Chapter 2
s: The children of Ammon are accused of insulting and reproaching the LORD's people and magnifying themselves against their border. They will become like Gomorrah, a perpetual desolation of nettles and salt pits, inherited by the survivors of the LORD's nation.

l: Assyria, The Book of Zephaniah, Chapter 2
s: The LORD will stretch out his hand against the north and destroy Assyria. Its fate is tied to the desolation of Nineveh.

l: Nineveh, The Book of Zephaniah, Chapter 2
s: Nineveh will be made a desolation, as dry as the wilderness, with herds and animals lying in its midst, and the pelican and porcupine lodging in its capitals. It is described as the joyous, careless city that said 'I am, and there is no one besides me,' and passersby will hiss and shake their fists at it.

l: humble of the land, The Book of Zephaniah, Chapter 2
s: The humble of the land, who have kept the LORD's ordinances, are urged to seek the LORD, righteousness, and humility. It may be that they will be hidden in the day of the LORD's anger.

l: day of the LORD's judgment, The Book of Zephaniah, Chapter 2
s: The day of the LORD's anger is an appointed time, when the day passes like chaff, and his fierce anger comes on the shameless nation. The humble are told they may be hidden on that day.

l: The Book of Zephaniah, The Book of Zephaniah, Chapter 3
s: Chapter 3 opens with a woe against the rebellious, polluted, oppressing city, whose princes, judges, prophets, and priests are corrupt even though the LORD within her is righteous and has shown her the fate of other nations. The LORD calls on those who wait for him to expect the day when he gathers the nations to pour out his indignation and the fire of his jealousy. After that he will purify the peoples' lips, bring offerings from beyond Cush's rivers, remove the proud, and leave an afflicted and poor remnant of Israel who take refuge in his name and live without lies or fear. The daughter of Zion is told to sing and rejoice because the LORD, a mighty one who saves, is among her, has removed her enemy, and will rejoice over her with singing. He promises to deal with her afflictors, save the lame, gather the driven away, and give them honor and praise when he restores their fortunes.

l: the LORD, The Book of Zephaniah, Chapter 3
s: The LORD is described as righteous within the city, bringing his justice to light every morning, and as having cut off nations as a warning that went unheeded. He announces that he will rise up to the prey, gather the nations to pour out his anger, purify the peoples' lips, remove the proud, save the lame, gather the driven away, and rejoice over Zion with singing as a mighty savior.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Zephaniah, Chapter 3
s: The city is called rebellious, polluted, and oppressing, since she did not obey, receive correction, trust the LORD, or draw near to God. Her princes are roaring lions, her judges evening wolves, her prophets treacherous, and her priests have profaned the sanctuary; the LORD nevertheless promises to remove her proud ones, take away her enemy, and honor her. Addressed as daughter of Jerusalem and Zion, she is told to rejoice and not fear, for the LORD is among her.

l: nations, The Book of Zephaniah, Chapter 3
s: The LORD says he has cut off nations, leaving their battlements and cities desolate and uninhabited. He also states that he will gather the nations and kingdoms to pour on them his indignation and fierce anger, and that all the earth will be devoured by the fire of his jealousy. Afterward he will purify the lips of the peoples so they call on his name and serve him shoulder to shoulder.

l: Israel, The Book of Zephaniah, Chapter 3
s: The remnant of Israel is promised that it will not do iniquity or speak lies, no deceitful tongue will be found in its mouth, and it will feed and lie down with no one making it afraid. Israel is told to shout and be glad because the LORD, the King of Israel, is among them and has thrown out the enemy.

l: afflicted and poor people, The Book of Zephaniah, Chapter 3
s: The LORD says he will leave an afflicted and poor people among the city after removing the proudly exulting ones. They will take refuge in the LORD's name, and they form the remnant that will live without deceit or fear.

l: day of the LORD's judgment, The Book of Zephaniah, Chapter 3
s: The LORD tells those who wait for him that it is the day he rises up to the prey, determined to gather the nations and kingdoms and pour on them his indignation and fierce anger. On it all the earth will be devoured by the fire of his jealousy, and it leads into the purifying of the peoples' lips and the removal of the proud from his holy mountain.

l: restoration of fortunes, The Book of Zephaniah, Chapter 3
s: The LORD promises that at that time he will bring the people in and gather them, giving them honor and praise among all the peoples of the earth. This will happen when he restores their fortunes before their eyes, reversing the shame of those who were lame and driven away.

l: Deuteronomy
s: This document is the book of Deuteronomy, a series of farewell addresses by Moses to all Israel in Moab, east of the Jordan, in the fortieth year, just before the people enter the land the LORD swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Its central figures are the LORD, Moses, the people of Israel, and Joshua, who is named as Moses' successor. It opens with Moses' historical review: the command at Horeb, the appointment of judges, the refusal at Kadesh Barnea and the resulting forty years of wandering, and the victories over Sihon and Og, whose land was given to Reubenites, Gadites, and half of Manasseh. Moses is barred from crossing the Jordan and may only view the land from Pisgah. He then urges obedience to the statutes and ordinances, warns against idols, and recites the ten commandments given at Horeb. He calls Israel to love the LORD with all heart, soul, and might, to teach the words to their children, and to remember the LORD's deliverance from Egypt. He warns against forgetting the LORD in prosperity, recalls the golden calf and the new tablets, and instructs Israel to destroy the Canaanite nations and their worship sites. A long law code follows. It covers worship at one chosen place, enticement to idolatry, clean and unclean food, tithes, debts, slaves, festivals, judges, kings, priests, prophets, cities of refuge, warfare, and many matters of family, sexual conduct, property, and justice for the vulnerable. First fruits and tithes are accompanied by confessions of the LORD's deliverance. Moses commands that the law be inscribed on stones at Mount Ebal, with blessing declared from Gerizim and curses from Ebal. A long list of blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience follows, ending in scattering and exile. A covenant is made in Moab, and Moses promises restoration if Israel returns, setting before them the choice of life or death. Moses, aged 120, commissions Joshua, has the law written and placed beside the ark, and teaches Israel a song warning of their future rebellion and the LORD's vengeance. He blesses the tribes one by one. He then climbs Mount Nebo, sees the land, and dies in Moab. He is buried in an unknown place, Israel mourns thirty days, Joshua leads them, and no prophet since has equaled Moses.

l: Moses, Deuteronomy
s: Moses is a man of God and servant of the LORD, brother of Aaron, who serves as Israel's leader, lawgiver, and mediator at the end of the wilderness years. The records open in the fortieth year beyond the Jordan, where he begins declaring the law, recounts events from Horeb to Kadesh, and recalls appointing heads of tribes as judges because he could not bear the people alone. He recounts defeating Sihon and Og and distributing the eastern land to Reubenites, Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. A central tension runs throughout: the LORD was angry with him for the people's sakes and, by decree and oath, barred him from crossing the Jordan, and he begged in vain to enter. He is told to view the land from Pisgah and commission Joshua. Later it is stated that he trespassed at Meribah of Kadesh by not upholding the LORD's holiness. Moses teaches the statutes and ordinances as commanded, warns against adding to or subtracting from them, and sets apart three cities of refuge. He recalls standing between the LORD and the people at Horeb, receiving two stone tablets, fasting forty days and nights without bread or water, breaking the tablets over the calf, and interceding for Israel and Aaron. He then cuts second tablets and makes an ark of acacia wood at the LORD's command. With the elders he commands the setting up of inscribed stones and an altar on Ebal, and assigns tribes to Gerizim and Ebal for blessing and curse. At age 120 he tells Israel he cannot cross, encourages Joshua, writes the law, orders its reading every seven years, and is told he will die and Israel will rebel. He writes and teaches a song, recites it with Joshua to all Israel, and charges them to teach the law to their children. He blesses each tribe, climbs Nebo to Pisgah, sees the whole land, and dies in Moab with undimmed eyes and undiminished strength. He is remembered as an unequaled prophet, known by the LORD face to face, who performed signs and wonders in Egypt.

l: Israel, Deuteronomy
s: Israel is the people addressed by Moses in these records: a chosen, holy people of the LORD, descended from the fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, grown from seventy persons who went to Egypt into a multitude like the stars, yet described as the fewest of all peoples. Also called Jeshurun, they were servants and slaves under Pharaoh in Egypt, witnessed plagues and wonders, and wandered forty years in the wilderness. The most important theme is covenant: the LORD chose them not for righteousness but by oath to the fathers, and requires them to fear, love, serve and cling to him alone, keep his commandments, and avoid other gods, idolatry, intermarriage and covenants with the nations. Equally prominent is their character as stiff-necked and rebellious from leaving Egypt onward, spared only through Moses' intercession. The account unfolds from Moses' reminders of the journey: refusal at Kadesh, circling Mount Seir, passing Edom, Moab and Ammon peacefully, and defeating Sihon and Og, whose land went to Reubenites, Gadites and half of Manasseh, leaving Israel near Beth Peor. Moses then recalls Horeb, where they feared the fire and voice, and sets out extended commands: destroy pagan worship sites, worship only at the chosen place, avoid blood, tithe, keep the feasts, appoint judges, punish idolatry, obey priests and the coming prophet, care for Levites, foreigners, orphans and widows, cancel debts, and conduct war and civil life justly. Ceremonies on Mounts Ebal and Gerizim and the covenant renewal make them the people of the LORD. Blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience are laid out, along with predictions that they will turn to other gods, be scattered, then return and be restored; they lack a heart to know as yet and are offered a choice of life or death. The law is to be read every seven years, and a song calls them a perverse generation who abandoned the Rock, yet promises compassion. It ends with Moses' blessing: Israel is happy, saved by the LORD, dwelling in safety in a land of grain and new wine, with enemies submitting.

l: the LORD your God, Deuteronomy
s: The LORD is the covenant God of Israel, presented throughout as one, unique and supreme: God of gods and Lord of lords, the only God in heaven and on earth, owner of heaven and earth, eternal, a Rock, with power over life and death. His character is paradoxical but consistent: a devouring fire and jealous God who repays those who hate him and will not pardon idolatry, yet also merciful, faithful, impartial, loving, and just toward the fatherless, widow and foreigner. What matters most is his covenant with Israel. He swore the land to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, chose Israel out of love for their fathers rather than for their number, redeemed them from Egypt's house of bondage with signs, wonders and a mighty hand, and declared them his own possession. He keeps covenant loving kindness to a thousand generations with those who love him and keep his commandments, and he visits iniquity on those who hate him. The records unfold from Horeb to the edge of the land. He commands Israel to take the land, goes before them in fire and cloud, and is angered by their unbelief, so the evil generation is barred from entering. He leads them forty years in the wilderness, humbling and testing them, feeding them manna, giving water from the rock, and disciplining them as a father disciplines a son. He gives the ten commandments, speaking from the fire and writing them on stone tablets, then rewrites them after the calf incident, when he heeds Moses' prayer. He delivers Sihon and Og as precedents, and he promises to drive out the nations of Canaan, going before Israel and fighting for them. He gives statutes on worship at the chosen place, the Levites, justice, warfare and daily life. He sets before Israel blessing for obedience and curses, plagues and scattering for disobedience. He foretells their forsaking him and the exile, yet also their gathering, the circumcision of their hearts, and the curses falling on their enemies. He is their life and the length of their days. The account closes with his song praising himself as Rock and Savior, his blessing of the tribes as the one who loves the people, and his showing Moses the land he swore to give. Moses is known face to face but dies outside it, according to the LORD's word.

l: Horeb, Deuteronomy
s: Horeb is a mountain where the LORD addressed Israel. In Chapter 1 he tells them they have stayed long enough and must set out to possess the land; Horeb is the start of an eleven-day journey to Kadesh Barnea via Mount Seir. In Chapter 4 the mountain burns with fire, and the LORD speaks from it, declaring his covenant and the ten commandments on two stone tablets.

l: Mount Seir, Deuteronomy
s: given_to Esau's descendants (children of Esau) [as a possession by the LORD] Israel encircles Mount Seir for many days until the LORD tells them to turn northward. The LORD had given it to Esau as a possession, so Israel may not take any of its land, and the Horites who once lived there were destroyed by Esau's descendants.

l: Kadesh Barnea, Deuteronomy
s: Kadesh Barnea is reached after travel through the great and terrible wilderness from Horeb. It is the place where Israel refuses to go up, and where they stay many days after their defeat.

l: Sihon, Deuteronomy
s: Sihon is the Amorite king of Heshbon. The LORD hardens his spirit, so he refuses Israel passage despite peace words, fights them with all his people, and is struck down with his sons and people, losing all his cities.

l: Og, Deuteronomy
s: Og was an Amorite king of Bashan and the last survivor of the Rephaim. He led his people against Israel at Edrei, where the LORD delivered them into Israel's hand and none remained. He is remembered for his iron bedstead, nine cubits long.

l: Amorites, Deuteronomy
s: The Amorites are named as the people whose hill country Israel is to enter, and Moses recalls that Sihon, king of the Amorites in Heshbon, was struck. When Israel presumptuously went up, the Amorites came out, chased them like bees, and beat them down in Seir as far as Hormah.

l: Bashan, Deuteronomy
s: Bashan, also called the land of Rephaim, was Og's kingdom with sixty fortified cities in Argob plus villages; Israel took it, gave it to half-tribe Manasseh, and Jair renamed Argob Havvoth Jair.

l: Moab, Deuteronomy
s: Moab is a land, with Ar as its border, given by the LORD to Lot's children. Israel is therefore told not to fight it and passes through the wilderness of Moab. Moabites call the earlier tall inhabitants Emim, and later sold Israel passage.

l: hill country of the Amorites, Deuteronomy
s: is_inhabited_by Amorites The hill country of the Amorites is the destination the LORD commands Israel to take, and Israel arrives at it by way of the wilderness. Israel refuses to go up, and later goes up against the LORD's warning and is defeated there.

l: Canaan, Deuteronomy
s: Canaan is the promised land lying across the Jordan, in the land of the Canaanites, which the LORD swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and gives to Israel as a possession and inheritance. It is described as a good land flowing with milk and honey, with hills and valleys that drink rain from the sky. Its borders run from the wilderness and Lebanon to the Euphrates in the east and to the western sea. It holds great and good cities, houses, cisterns, vineyards, and olive trees that Israel did not build or plant, along with brooks, springs, and underground water. It produces wheat, barley, vines, figs, pomegranates, olives, and honey, and has stones of iron and hills yielding copper, so nothing is lacking. The records unfold as a progression of promise, conditions, and warning. Early on, the land is set before Israel, but the unbelieving generation will not see it except Caleb, while Joshua and the little ones will enter. Moses will see it from Mount Nebo but not enter. Israel is to possess it by driving out nations greater and mightier, gradually, and this is due to the nations' wickedness and the LORD's oath, not Israel's righteousness. The land is the place to keep the commandments; long life there depends on faithfulness, honoring parents, and loving and obeying the LORD. Israel must not forget the LORD when full, and idolatry would mean removal. It is the site of the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal near Gilgal. The worshipper offers its first fruit and confesses the LORD's gift. Obedience brings blessing in barns and work, while disobedience turns the sky to bronze and earth to iron, with produce eaten by locusts and worms, and the people plucked from it. Finally, the scattered Israelites are promised return to possess it again, and Israel is told obeying the law will prolong their days there.

l: twelve spies, Deuteronomy
s: consists_of twelve men [one man for every tribe] Moses takes twelve men, one from each tribe, at Israel's request to search the land. They go up to the valley of Eshcol, bring back some of its fruit, and report that it is a good land the LORD gives.

l: Egypt, Deuteronomy
s: Egypt is a land ruled by Pharaoh, remembered chiefly as Israel's house of bondage. Its irrigated-by-foot soil is contrasted with the rain-fed promised land of Canaan. Israel's forefather, a Syrian ready to perish, went down there, few in number, and grew into a great, populous nation. The Egyptians then mistreated and afflicted them with hard labor. The LORD brought the people out with a mighty hand, signs, and wonders against Pharaoh and his land, and the Red Sea overflowed its army, horses, and chariots as they pursued. Egypt also stands for feared boils and diseases. The account ends in warning: the LORD will bring the Israelites back in ships as slaves whom nobody will buy.

l: Caleb, Deuteronomy
s: Caleb, son of Jephunneh, wholly followed the LORD; therefore he is exempted from the oath against the evil generation and promised to see the land and receive the ground he trod, with his children.

l: Joshua, Deuteronomy
s: Joshua, son of Nun, is Moses' designated successor, commissioned to lead Israel across the Jordan into the promised land and cause the people to inherit it. Early on he is described as one who stands before Moses and will enter the land, and Moses is told to encourage him. Moses then charges him not to fear, recalling what the LORD did to the two kings. At the Tent of Meeting the LORD commissions him, and Moses charges him before all Israel to be strong and courageous. Finally, he is full of the spirit of wisdom through Moses' laying on of hands, and Israel obeys him.

l: Israel's rebellion at Kadesh, Deuteronomy
s: At Kadesh Barnea, Israel refuses the command to go up, fearing fortified cities and Anakim. Despite Moses' reminders they disbelieve, and the LORD swears judgment, excluding that generation except Caleb from the promised land; they then presume to attack and are routed.

l: commandments, statutes, and ordinances, Deuteronomy
s: The commandments, statutes, and ordinances are the body of law that Moses teaches Israel on the LORD's behalf. They are unalterable: nothing may be added or removed. Keeping them counts as righteousness before the LORD and as Israel's wisdom and understanding in the sight of the peoples, who will see that no other great nation has such righteous law. Their purpose is Israel's good and preservation. The account unfolds in stages. In Chapter 4 Moses teaches them and forbids adding or subtracting. In Chapter 5 he calls Israel to hear them, and the LORD has Moses stay beside him to receive all of them for teaching. Chapter 6 says they are given so Israel may do them in the land, fear the LORD, and live long and well. They are to be taught diligently, bound on hand and forehead, and written on door posts and gates. Chapters 7, 8, and 11 make obedience the condition for the covenant's loving kindness and for blessings: life, multiplying, possessing the land, rain, fruitfulness, and victory. Forgetting the LORD or turning to other gods brings perishing and drought. Chapter 28 sets blessings for keeping them against curses for failing, with fearing the LORD's name as the aim. Chapter 30 declares the commandment not too hard or distant but very near, in the mouth and heart, centered on loving the LORD and walking in his ways. Chapter 31 closes with Moses writing the law in a book, giving it to the priests and elders, and ordering it read to all Israel every seven years at the feast of booths. The Levites place it beside the ark as a witness against Israel.

l: Esau's descendants (children of Esau), Deuteronomy
s: Esau's descendants, kin to Israel, live in Seir, given to them by the LORD. They once destroyed the Horites and settled there; Israel is told not to contend with them or take their land, only buy food and water.

l: Ammonites, Deuteronomy
s: The Ammonites are descendants of Lot whose land the LORD gave them as a possession. Israel is forbidden to trouble them or take it. The land was once Rephaim territory, called Zamzummim by Ammonites, destroyed by the LORD; Israel stays away, including the Jabbok banks.

l: Gilead, Deuteronomy
s: Gilead was taken with the other cities of the plain and Bashan. Half the hill country of Gilead went to the Reubenites and Gadites, the rest to the half-tribe of Manasseh, and Gilead was also given to Machir.

l: battle at Jahaz, Deuteronomy
s: Battle at Jahaz: Sihon and all his people attacked Israel; the LORD delivered Sihon up, Israel struck down him, his sons and people, then took all his cities.

l: Reubenites, Deuteronomy
s: possesses Gilead [half the hill country, with Gadites] The Reubenites received land from Aroer by the Arnon valley and half the hill country of Gilead, extending to the Jabbok, along with the Arabah and Jordan border. Their men of valor were commanded to cross the Jordan armed before their brothers, while their families and livestock stayed in the cities.

l: Gadites, Deuteronomy
s: possesses Gilead [half the hill country, with Reubenites] The Gadites, together with the Reubenites, received land from Aroer and half the hill country of Gilead to the Jabbok, plus the Arabah and the Jordan and its border. Their men of valor were to cross over armed ahead of their brothers until the other tribes received rest.

l: Manasseh, Deuteronomy
s: possesses Bashan [half-tribe; given by Moses] The half-tribe of Manasseh was given the rest of Gilead and all Bashan, the kingdom of Og, including all the region of Argob. Jair the son of Manasseh took the Argob region and named it Havvoth Jair after himself.

l: Mount Nebo, Deuteronomy
s: Mount Nebo is a mountain in the Abarim range in Moab, across from Jericho, with Pisgah at its top. The LORD tells Moses to climb it, see Canaan from afar, and die there. Moses then ascends from the plains of Moab to Pisgah and is shown the whole land he will not enter.

l: cities of Bashan (Og), Deuteronomy
s: Sixty fortified cities in Argob, with high walls, gates, bars, and many unwalled villages, formed Og's kingdom; Israel captured and utterly destroyed them all, keeping livestock and plunder.

l: conquest of Og, Deuteronomy
s: Battle at Edrei where Og attacked Israel; the LORD delivered him into Israel's hand, they destroyed his people entirely, captured all sixty cities and plunder, and took land from Arnon to Hermon.

l: Moses' request to enter the land, Deuteronomy
s: has_outcome denied [LORD refused] Moses begged the LORD, praising his greatness and incomparable works, to let him cross the Jordan and see the good land, the fine mountain, and Lebanon. The LORD, angry because of the people, refused and told him to speak no more of it, but to go up to Pisgah and view the land in every direction and to commission Joshua.

l: stone tablets of the covenant, Deuteronomy
s: The stone tablets of the covenant were written by the LORD's own finger with the ten commandments, containing all the words spoken on the mountain. The first set was given to Moses after forty days and nights, but he broke them upon seeing the calf.
