The LORD then had Moses cut two new tablets, rewrote the same words, and Moses placed them in the ark, where they remain.

l: carved images and idolatry, Deuteronomy
s: is_punished_by destruction and scattering [Israel would perish from the land and be scattered] Israel is forbidden to make a carved image in the form of any figure, whether human, animal, bird, creeping thing, or fish, since they saw no form at Horeb. They are also warned not to be drawn into worshiping the sun, moon, and stars. Idolatry is said to bring utter destruction and scattering, with exile among gods of wood and stone that cannot see, hear, eat, or smell.

l: three cities of refuge, Deuteronomy
s: Three cities of refuge are set apart so that a man who kills his neighbor unintentionally, without prior hatred, can flee there and live, preventing innocent blood from being shed. Chapter 4 names them beyond the Jordan: Bezer for the Reubenites, Ramoth for the Gadites, Golan for the Manassites. Chapter 19 sets three cities in the middle of the land, with roads prepared and the land divided in three, and adds three more if the border is enlarged.

l: covenant (at Horeb), Deuteronomy
s: A covenant the LORD made at Horeb, stressed by Moses as made not with the fathers but with the living Israelites present that day, its content being the commandments spoken from the fire.

l: Ten Commandments, Deuteronomy
s: The Ten Commandments are words the LORD spoke to the whole assembly of Israel from the fire on the mountain, written on two stone tablets and given to Moses. They forbid other gods, images, misusing the LORD's name, murder, adultery, stealing, false testimony and coveting, and require Sabbath observance and honoring parents. They are recited first, then rewritten on new tablets matching the first.

l: other gods, Deuteronomy
s: Other gods are the deities of surrounding and distant peoples, unknown to Israel and its fathers. Their gold and silver images are an abomination to the LORD. Chapter 7 warns that intermarriage could lead Israel's sons to serve them, kindling the LORD's anger and becoming a snare, so engraved images must be burned. Chapter 13 shows prophets, secret enticers, and wicked city fellows all calling Israel to serve them.

l: Sabbath day, Deuteronomy
s: The Sabbath is the seventh day, a holy day of rest to the LORD. After six days of labor, no one works: people, household, servants, animals, or strangers. It commemorates Israel's deliverance from servitude in Egypt by a mighty hand, so servants may rest too.

l: son (the Israelite's son), Deuteronomy
s: is_taught_by Israel [parents teach diligently] The son is to be taught the LORD's words diligently by his parent, together with later generations. When he asks what the testimonies, statutes, and ordinances mean, he is to be told of Israel's slavery in Egypt, the LORD's deliverance, and the purpose of the laws for their good.

l: signs and wonders in Egypt, Deuteronomy
s: The LORD's great signs and wonders against Pharaoh and his house, done with a mighty hand to bring Israel out of Egypt into the sworn land; Israel must not forget them and should recount them to a son asking about the laws.

l: seven nations of Canaan, Deuteronomy
s: Seven nations (Hittite, Girgashite, Amorite, Canaanite, Perizzite, Hivite, Jebusite), greater and mightier than Israel. The LORD will gradually expel and destroy them, delivering their kings to Israel, which must make no covenants, marriages, or mercy toward them.

l: idolatrous objects (altars, pillars, Asherah poles, engraved images), Deuteronomy
s: The Israelites are commanded to break down the nations' altars, dash their pillars in pieces, cut down their Asherah poles, and burn their engraved images with fire. They must not covet or take the silver and gold on the images, nor bring an abomination into their house. Doing so would make them a devoted thing like it, so they must utterly detest and abhor it.

l: covenant (oath to the fathers), Deuteronomy
s: The LORD's desire to keep the oath he swore to Israel's fathers is given as a reason for bringing Israel out of Egypt. The LORD keeps covenant and loving kindness to a thousand generations with those who love him and keep his commandments. If Israel listens to and keeps the ordinances, he will keep the covenant and loving kindness with them. Israel itself is forbidden to make a covenant with the nations of the land.

l: utter destruction of the nations, Deuteronomy
s: is_commanded_for seven nations of Canaan When the LORD delivers the nations up and Israel strikes them, Israel is commanded to utterly destroy them, showing no mercy and no pity. The text says the nations will be consumed little by little rather than at once, and that no one will be able to stand before Israel until they are destroyed. The reason given is to prevent covenants, marriages, and idolatry that would turn Israel from the LORD.

l: blessings of obedience, Deuteronomy
s: Chapter 7 promises that if Israel obeys the ordinances, the LORD will love, bless, and multiply them, bless offspring, land produce and livestock above all peoples, prevent barrenness, and remove sickness and Egypt's diseases, placing them on haters.

l: wilderness, Deuteronomy
s: has_feature venomous snakes and scorpions [great and terrible; thirsty ground without water] The wilderness is where the LORD led the Israelites for forty years to humble and test them and to learn what was in their hearts. It is described as great and terrible, with venomous snakes, scorpions, and thirsty ground. There the LORD fed them with manna, brought water out of flint rock, and kept their clothing from growing old and their feet from swelling.

l: other gods, Deuteronomy
s: The LORD foretells that Israel will play the prostitute after the strange gods of the land, serving them, despising him, and breaking his covenant. This turning to other gods is given as the cause of the LORD hiding his face and of the evils that will come on Israel.

l: nations of the land, Deuteronomy
s: The nations of the land are peoples mightier and greater than Israel, with heavily fortified cities and tall Anakim among them. They are marked by wickedness and abominations, including child sacrifice by fire and heeding sorcerers and diviners. Early on, the LORD promises to destroy them and drive them out before Israel. Later, Israel is told to destroy their worship sites and avoid their gods, and finally the nations are again shown driven out because of their abominations.

l: molten calf, Deuteronomy
s: A molten calf made by Israel after turning from the LORD's way; Moses burned it, ground it to fine dust, and threw the dust into the mountain brook, destroying it.

l: Israel's rebellion and the golden calf sin, Deuteronomy
s: provoked the LORD your God [to anger, wanting to destroy them] Israel's rebellion is traced from leaving Egypt onward, with the calf at Horeb as its central instance, provoking the LORD's anger to the point of threatened destruction. Further provocations are named at Taberah, Massah, Kibroth Hattaavah, and Kadesh Barnea, where they did not believe or obey the LORD. The LORD was also angry enough to destroy Aaron, for whom Moses prayed.

l: Israel's righteousness, Deuteronomy
s: is_not_reason_for possession of the land Moses insists that Israel's righteousness and the uprightness of its heart are not the reason it possesses the land, and warns them not to say so in their hearts. He states they are a stiff-necked people, and the reasons for the gift are the nations' wickedness and the LORD's oath to the patriarchs.

l: ark (Moses' ark of acacia wood), Deuteronomy
s: The ark is a chest of acacia wood that Moses made at the LORD's command to hold the new tablets; he placed them inside after descending the mountain, they remain there, and Levi's tribe bears it as the ark of the covenant.

l: Levi, Deuteronomy
s: Levi is a tribe set apart by the LORD to carry the ark of the covenant, minister before him, and bless in his name. It has no portion or inheritance among its brothers, since the LORD himself is its inheritance. In Moses' blessing, Levi holds the Thummim and Urim, was proved at Massah, and put loyalty to the LORD's word and covenant above family. Levi will teach Jacob the ordinances and Israel the law, offer incense and whole burnt offerings, and Moses asks that the LORD bless and defend it.

l: Israel's requirements of devotion, Deuteronomy
s: Moses states that the LORD requires Israel to fear him, walk in all his ways, love him, and serve him with all their heart and soul. They must keep his commandments and statutes for their own good, circumcise their heart, no longer be stiff-necked, cling to him, and swear by his name. They are also to love the foreigner, remembering they were foreigners in Egypt.

l: Israelites (addressees of Moses), Deuteronomy
s: The Israelites are the addressees of Moses, witnesses of the LORD's signs in Egypt, the Red Sea, and the wilderness. They are commanded to love him and keep his commandments always, teaching them to their children and displaying them. About to cross the Jordan and possess Canaan, they face blessing for obedience, curse for disobedience, and warning against deceived hearts serving other gods.

l: blessing and curse, Deuteronomy
s: Blessing and curse is the paired choice Moses sets before the Israelites, depending on whether they listen to the LORD's voice and keep his commandments or go after other gods. In Chapter 11 the blessing is to be set on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal once they enter the land. Chapter 28 describes the blessings in detail: prosperity in city and field, offspring, livestock, rain, victory over enemies, and lending to nations. Chapter 30 returns to the pair, says the curses fall on the Israelites' enemies, and closes by framing them as life and death.

l: Mount Gerizim, Deuteronomy
s: Mount Gerizim is a mountain beyond the Jordan near the oaks of Moreh, where, after crossing the Jordan, the tribes of Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin stand to bless the people.

l: Mount Ebal, Deuteronomy
s: Mount Ebal is a place in Chapter 27 where Israel sets up law-inscribed plastered stones and builds the LORD's altar of uncut stones, and where Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan and Naphtali stand for the curse.

l: Levites, Deuteronomy
s: The Levites are the tribe of Levi, priests and Levites together, set apart among the Israelites. They receive no land portion or inheritance among their brothers; the LORD himself is their inheritance, and they live on his offerings made by fire. They dwell within Israelite town gates, and the Israelites are repeatedly told not to forsake them as long as they live in the land. In the third year they share the stored tithe with the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow, and they rejoice and eat before the LORD at the chosen place. The LORD chose them to stand and minister in his name. A Levite from any town may come to the chosen place and minister like his fellow Levites, receiving equal portions. In the end, the Levitical priests join Moses in addressing Israel as the LORD's people, and the Levites declare the curses aloud to all Israel, who respond 'Amen'.

l: place the LORD shall choose, Deuteronomy
s: The place the LORD shall choose is the single location, within one of the tribes' territories across the Jordan, where the LORD your God causes his name to dwell. It is the only permitted site for burnt offerings and sacrifices. Chapter 12 requires all offerings, tithes, vows and firstborn animals be brought there. Chapter 14 has tithes eaten there with rejoicing, or money carried if distant. Chapter 16 adds Passover, feasts, and appearances before him.

l: pagan worship sites and objects, Deuteronomy
s: is_located_at high mountains, hills, under green trees [places where nations served their gods] The nations' places on high mountains, hills and under green trees are to be destroyed. Their altars are to be broken down, pillars dashed in pieces, Asherah poles burned and engraved images cut down, so that their name is destroyed from the place.

l: offerings and sacrifices, Deuteronomy
s: must_be_eaten_at chosen place of worship [tithes, firstborn, vows, free will offerings, not within gates] Burnt offerings, sacrifices, tithes, wave offerings, vows, free will offerings and firstborn of herd and flock must be brought to the chosen place and not offered anywhere else. The Israelites eat the eligible portions there before the LORD and rejoice. The blood and meat of burnt offerings are offered on the LORD's altar.

l: eating of meat, Deuteronomy
s: is_permitted within all gates [according to desire, clean and unclean alike] The Israelites may kill and eat meat within their gates as their desire leads, as with the gazelle and deer, and the clean and unclean may eat it alike. This permission holds when the border is enlarged or the chosen place is too far away, but it does not extend to the tithes, firstborn, vows and offerings, which must be eaten at the chosen place.

l: blood, Deuteronomy
s: is the life [must not be eaten with the meat] The Israelites are forbidden to eat blood because the blood is the life, and the life must not be eaten with the meat. It is to be poured out on the earth like water, and obedience is tied to things going well for them and their children. Blood from sacrifices is poured out on the LORD's altar.

l: land, Deuteronomy
s: The land is the territory the LORD gives Israel to possess and inherit, described as flowing with milk and honey and lying across the Jordan. It was sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob for their offspring. Records first stress entering it by crossing the Jordan, setting up stones and an altar, dividing it for cities of refuge, forbidding innocent bloodshed and moving ancient landmarks. The LORD predicts Israel will grow fat there and turn to other gods. At the end Moses sees its full extent from Pisgah, from Gilead to Zoar, but will not cross into it.

l: prophet or dreamer of dreams, Deuteronomy
s: A prophet or dreamer of dreams who may give a sign or wonder that comes to pass, yet urges following other gods; he must not be heeded and is put to death for rebellion against the LORD, removing evil from the people.

l: secret enticer (close relative or friend), Deuteronomy
s: A close relation or friend who secretly entices others to serve other gods. The person enticed must show no consent, pity, or concealment, and must kill him by stoning, hand first, then all the people, for seeking to draw them from the LORD.

l: idolatrous city, Deuteronomy
s: A hypothetical city whose inhabitants are reported to have been drawn by wicked fellows to serve other gods. The people must diligently investigate; if the report is true, inhabitants and livestock are killed by sword, plunder is burned with the city as an offering to the LORD, and it remains a heap forever, never rebuilt.

l: death penalty for idolatry, Deuteronomy
s: Chapter 13 prescribes death for idolatry: the prophet or dreamer urging other gods, the secret enticer among kin or friends, and a drawn-away city. The enticer is stoned, accuser's hand first; the city is struck by sword and burned, removing evil and making all Israel hear and fear.

l: clean animals, Deuteronomy
s: Clean animals are those with split hooves that chew the cud, such as ox, sheep, goat, and deer; the records also permit water creatures with fins and scales, and all clean birds, as food.

l: unclean animals, Deuteronomy
s: Unclean animals are a category of creatures that may not be eaten. Chapter 14 lists the camel, hare and rabbit (chew cud, hoof not parted) and the pig (split hoof, no cud), then finfless water creatures, named birds, and winged creeping things; the pig's carcass may not be touched.

l: dietary laws, Deuteronomy
s: Dietary laws in Chapter 14 permit animals that part the hoof and chew the cud, finned and scaled fish, and clean birds, while forbidding listed unclean ones. They bar eating what dies of itself (allowed for foreigners) and boiling a kid in its mother's milk, grounded in Israel's holiness.

l: foreigner, Deuteronomy
s: is_entitled_to justice [may not be deprived of it] The foreigner is protected from being deprived of justice and is counted among poor hired servants who must be paid promptly. Forgotten sheaves, olive boughs, and vineyard gleanings are left for him. Israel is told to remember it was a slave in Egypt.

l: tithe, Deuteronomy
s: The tithe is a yearly offering of one's seed increase, grain, wine, oil, and firstborn livestock, eaten before the LORD at his chosen place to teach fear of him. If the journey is too long, it may be converted to money and spent there. Every third year it is stored in town gates for Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows.

l: firstborn of the herd and flock, Deuteronomy
s: Firstborn males of herd and flock are dedicated to the LORD and exempt from work and shearing. Each year the owner and household eat them before the LORD at the chosen place. Defective animals, lame or blind, are not sacrificed but eaten within the gates by clean and unclean alike, blood poured on the ground like water.

l: seventh-year release of debts, Deuteronomy
s: A release of debts proclaimed by the LORD every seventh year: creditors must release what they lent to fellow Israelites and not demand payment, though foreigners may still be required to pay. Refusing to lend as the seventh year nears is warned against as sin.

l: creditor (the lender among the Israelites), Deuteronomy
s: The creditor must release what he has lent to his neighbor and brother in the seventh year, though he may still require payment from a foreigner. He is told not to harden his heart or shut his hand toward a poor brother, to lend sufficient for the need, and not to hold back because the release year is near. He is to give without a grieving heart, because the LORD will bless him for it.

l: poor brother (the needy fellow Israelite), Deuteronomy
s: The poor brother is to receive an open hand and a loan sufficient for his need, and must not be refused because the year of release is near. If refused, he may cry to the LORD against the lender, and it would be sin to the lender. The text says the poor will never cease out of the land.

l: Hebrew servant (the slave sold to a fellow Israelite), Deuteronomy
s: A Hebrew man or woman sold to a fellow Israelite serves six years and goes free in the seventh, not empty-handed but liberally furnished from the master's flock, threshing floor, and wine press. If the servant says he will not leave because he loves the master and his house, the master pierces his ear with an awl to the door and he serves forever. The master is told the servant has been worth double a hired hand.

l: release of slaves in the seventh year, Deuteronomy
s: A command that in the seventh year a Hebrew servant who has served six years be freed. The master must give liberally from flock, threshing floor and wine press, not send him away empty, remembering Egypt's slavery and redemption, trusting the LORD's blessing.

l: Passover, Deuteronomy
s: Passover is a observance kept to the LORD in the month of Abib. Its animal is sacrificed from flock and herd at the chosen place, never within the people's own gates, at evening at sunset, recalling leaving Egypt. It is roasted and eaten there, with no meat left until morning, then the people return to their tents.

l: feast of unleavened bread, Deuteronomy
s: The feast of unleavened bread is a seven-day observance commemorating the hasty departure from Egypt. Unleavened bread of affliction is eaten with Passover, no yeast may be seen within borders, the seventh day is a solemn assembly without work, and males appear before the LORD.

l: feast of weeks, Deuteronomy
s: The feast of weeks is a festival that begins after counting seven weeks from first putting the sickle to standing grain. It is kept with a free will offering according to the LORD's blessing, and with rejoicing at the chosen place by the whole household, Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow.

l: feast of booths, Deuteronomy
s: The feast of booths lasts seven days, following the gathering from the threshing floor and wine press. Held at the place the LORD chooses, the whole household, Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow rejoice as the LORD blesses their increase; it is the third feast males attend.

l: judges and officers, Deuteronomy
s: Judges and officers are appointed in all gates by tribe, then charged to judge righteously, without perverting justice, showing partiality, or taking bribes.

l: justice, Deuteronomy
s: Justice is a commanded standard that must be followed fully: it must not be perverted, show partiality, or accept bribes, which blind the wise and distort the righteous. Pursuing it is tied to living and inheriting the land the LORD gives.

l: children of Israel, Deuteronomy
s: Israel is the covenant community and people of the LORD, also the land they inhabit. It must root out idolatry and put away those who defy priest or judge, and may one day have a LORD-chosen king. After mourning Moses thirty days in Moab, the children of Israel obey Joshua.

l: Levitical priests, Deuteronomy
s: The Levitical priests minister before the LORD at the chosen place. With the judge they give verdicts on cases too hard for local courts; their rulings must be obeyed, and presumptuous refusal to listen means death. They also hold the law from which the king copies his own book.

l: judge (those days), Deuteronomy
s: gives_verdict_in hard cases in judgment [binding; not to be departed from right or left] The judge who serves in those days sits with the priests at the chosen place and gives verdicts on hard cases brought up from the gates. His sentence must be followed without turning right or left, and presumptuous disobedience to him is punishable by death.

l: king, Deuteronomy
s: The king is a ruler chosen by the LORD from among the people's brothers, never a foreigner. He is restricted from multiplying horses, wives, silver and gold, and from returning the people to Egypt. Upon taking the throne he writes his own copy of the law from the Levitical priests' book and reads it all his life, learning to fear the LORD and not exalt himself above his brothers, so he and his children prolong their rule in Israel.

l: idolater (man or woman who serves other gods), Deuteronomy
s: An idolater is a man or woman who breaks the Lord's covenant by serving other gods, sun, moon, or stars. Once reported, the matter is investigated; if certain, the person is stoned at the gates to remove evil from the people.

l: witnesses, Deuteronomy
s: Witnesses are a legal requirement: two or three are needed to establish any matter, and one witness alone is never enough. In capital cases, the witnesses' hands are first on the condemned, then all the people's. Chapter 17 sets the death-sentence rule; chapter 19 extends it to any iniquity or sin.

l: law, Deuteronomy
s: The law is to be taught by the Levitical priests and followed without turning right or left. The king must copy it into a book from the priests' copy and read it all his life to learn to fear the LORD and keep its words and statutes. Keeping it is tied to the king not being lifted up above his brothers and to long reigns for him and his children.

l: hard cases in judgment, Deuteronomy
s: is_referred_to place the LORD chooses [when too hard for local judgment] Matters too hard to decide locally, such as between blood and blood, plea and plea, or stroke and stroke, are to be taken up to the place the LORD chooses. There the Levitical priests and the judge give a verdict that must be followed exactly. Anyone who presumptuously ignores it is to die.

l: prophet (the coming prophet like Moses), Deuteronomy
s: The LORD promises to raise up this prophet from among Israel's brothers, like Moses, and to put his words in his mouth so that he speaks all that the LORD commands. Israel must listen to him, and the LORD will require an account from anyone who refuses.

l: false prophet, Deuteronomy
s: A false prophet speaks presumptuously in the LORD's name what He did not command, or speaks in other gods' names. Such a prophet is identified by unfulfilled predictions, which show the LORD did not speak, so Israel need not fear him; the penalty is death.

l: priests' due, Deuteronomy
s: The priests' due is the share given to priests: from ox or sheep sacrifices, the shoulder, two cheeks and inner parts; plus first fruits of grain, new wine, oil, and the first of the sheep's fleece.

l: occult practices, Deuteronomy
s: Occult practices, including child sacrifice by fire, divination, fortune-telling, enchanting, sorcery, charming, consulting familiar spirits, wizardry, and necromancy, are forbidden to Israel; the records conclude that whoever does them is an abomination to the LORD.

l: man slayer (unintentional killer), Deuteronomy
s: A man slayer unintentionally kills his neighbor without prior hatred, like an ax head slipping from its handle. Since he is not worthy of death, he may flee to one of the cities and live, protected from pursuit.

l: neighbor (of the man slayer), Deuteronomy
s: The neighbor is the one killed, either accidentally, as when an ax head flies off the handle in the forest, or deliberately by someone who hated him and lay in wait. The text also commands that his landmark, set by those of old, not be removed.

l: avenger of blood, Deuteronomy
s: may_pursue man slayer (unintentional killer) [in hot anger, if no refuge city existed] The avenger of blood might pursue a man slayer in hot anger and kill him on the long road, though the man was not worthy of death, which is why the cities of refuge are provided. If the killer was a deliberate murderer, the elders deliver him into the avenger's hand to die.

l: intentional murderer, Deuteronomy
s: An intentional murderer hates his neighbor, lies in wait, and strikes him mortally. Fleeing to a city of refuge gives no protection: the elders of his city send for him and hand him to the avenger of blood to die, without pity, purging innocent blood from Israel.

l: false witness, Deuteronomy
s: receives_penalty what he intended for the accused [when judges find he testified falsely] An unrighteous witness who testifies wrongdoing against someone is brought before the LORD, the priests, and the judges, who inquire diligently. If he is found to have testified falsely against his brother, he receives the penalty he intended for him, so that the evil is removed and others fear to repeat it.

l: law of retribution, Deuteronomy
s: states life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot [without pity] The chapter closes with the principle that the eye shall not pity: life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot. It is applied here to the false witness, who is to suffer what he planned for his brother.

l: enemies (Israel's enemies), Deuteronomy
s: Israel's enemies may have horses, chariots and greater numbers, yet Israel is told not to be afraid of them. The LORD goes with Israel to fight against them and save Israel.

l: priest (who addresses Israel before battle), Deuteronomy
s: The priest approaches the people as they draw near to battle and tells them to hear, not to let their hearts faint, and not to fear or tremble. He assures them that the LORD goes with them to fight for them and save them.

l: officers (who address the people), Deuteronomy
s: The officers speak to the people announcing exemptions for those with a new undedicated house, an unused vineyard, a betrothed but untaken wife, or a fearful and faint heart. When they finish, they appoint captains of armies at the head of the people.

l: battle, Deuteronomy
s: Battle is the occasion for which Israel is prepared by the priest's encouragement and the officers' exemptions. Men could die in it, which is why some are sent home, and captains are appointed to lead the people once the speeches end.

l: exemptions from battle, Deuteronomy
s: Chapter 20 lists four categories of men who may return home from battle: the owner of an undedicated new house, the planter of a vineyard whose fruit is unused, the man betrothed but not yet married, and the fearful and faint-hearted. Reasons: another would otherwise take the house, fruit or wife, and fear would spread to others.

l: city (besieged city), Deuteronomy
s: A city Israel approaches must first be offered peace. If it answers peacefully and opens, its people become forced laborers; if it makes war, it is besieged, and when delivered all its males are struck with the sword and its women, children, livestock and plunder taken. Bulwarks are built against it until it falls.

l: cities far off, Deuteronomy
s: Cities very far from Israel, not among the Canaanite nations' cities, fall under the peace-or-siege rule; if they refuse peace and fall, males are killed and women, children, livestock and plunder are taken.

l: cities of the nations of Canaan, Deuteronomy
s: Cities of Canaan's nations (Hittite, Amorite, Canaanite, Perizzite, Hivite, Jebusite), given to Israel as inheritance, must be utterly destroyed, nothing breathing spared, so Israel won't learn their abominations and sin.
